subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Menopause is the permanent cessation of ovarian estrogen production, diagnosed after 12 months of amenorrhoea in women >45 y. It marks transition to a low‑estrogen state with systemic effects.

sections.p: Menopause is defined as 12 consecutive months without menstrual bleeding, not caused by surgery, medication or illness, confirming ovarian failure.
b: Age 45‑55 y is typical; >55 y suggests premature ovarian insufficiency.
Serum FSH >30 IU/L on two occasions 4 weeks apart supports diagnosis when history is unclear.

t.b: Is ovarian reserve exhausted? High FSH indicates loss of feedback inhibition.
Confirms low estrogen state. Very low levels (<20 pg/mL) are typical.

sections.p: The STRAW+10 staging system categorises reproductive ageing; menopause is the “final menstrual period” (FMP) stage.
b: Early transition: variable cycle length, FSH 10‑25 IU/L.
Late transition: >60 days amenorrhoea, FSH >25 IU/L.
Post‑menopause: >12 mo amenorrhoea, FSH >30 IU/L.

sections.p: Most women experience natural ovarian follicular depletion; secondary causes must be excluded.
b: Natural ovarian senescence (most common).
Surgical oophorectomy or radiation.
Chemotherapy‑induced ovarian failure.
Autoimmune oophoritis (rare, more in low‑resource settings).
Infections (HIV, TB) that damage ovarian tissue.

sections.p: The estrogen decline produces vasomotor, genitourinary and metabolic symptoms, often affecting quality of life.
b: Hot flashes, night sweats, sleep disturbance.
Vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary urgency.
Bone loss → increased fracture risk.
Mood changes, decreased libido.

sections.p: Targeted tests confirm menopause, assess complications, and rule out mimics.
b: FSH, estradiol, TSH, prolactin when menstrual history unclear.
Bone mineral density (DEXA) for osteoporosis risk.
Transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness >4 mm after menopause warrants further evaluation.

t.b: Is there osteopenia/osteoporosis? Low BMD predicts fracture risk.
Is endometrium thickened? >4 mm may indicate hyperplasia or cancer.

sections.p: Certain findings require urgent evaluation for serious disease.
b: Unexpected vaginal bleeding → endometrial cancer.
Severe osteoporosis with fracture.
Cardiovascular events (MI, stroke) accelerated by estrogen loss.

sections.p: Treat symptoms, prevent long‑term sequelae, and address modifiable risk factors.
b: Lifestyle: regular weight‑bearing exercise, smoking cessation, adequate calcium/vitamin D.
Hormone therapy (systemic estrogen ± progestogen) for moderate‑to‑severe vasomotor symptoms, unless contraindicated (history of breast cancer, thromboembolism, active liver disease).
Non‑hormonal options: SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin, clonidine for hot flashes.
Topical vaginal estrogen for genitourinary syndrome, avoiding systemic exposure.
Bisphosphonates or denosumab for osteoporosis when BMD T‑score ≤ ‑2.5.
Annual review of symptoms, blood pressure, lipid profile.
DEXA every 2‑3 y after age 65 or earlier if risk factors.
Screen for breast and colorectal cancer per local guidelines.
Hyperthyroidism – causes heat intolerance, sweating.
Pituitary adenoma – can cause amenorrhoea.
Premature ovarian insufficiency – similar labs but younger age.
FSH may be normal in early transition; repeat testing is needed.
Endometrial thickness can be falsely low in obese patients due to technical limits.
Serum estradiol assays vary; low‑sensitivity tests may miss residual estrogen.

whenToSeekHelp: Vaginal bleeding after 12 months of amenorrhoea
Sudden severe bone pain or fracture
New onset chest pain, dyspnoea or neurological deficit

faq.a: No; once ovarian follicles are depleted, estrogen production cannot be restored without hormone therapy.

faq.q: Is hormone therapy safe for all women?
faq.a: It is contraindicated in women with a history of breast cancer, thromboembolism, active liver disease, or uncontrolled hypertension.

faq.q: Why is endometrial thickness measured after menopause?
faq.a: Low estrogen thins the lining; thickening may signal hyperplasia or cancer needing further assessment.

exam: Describe the diagnostic criteria for menopause and the role of FSH.
List three non‑hormonal treatments for vasomotor symptoms and their mechanisms.
Explain how you would evaluate post‑menopausal vaginal bleeding.
